objects.description:
Multi-stage Android malware impersonating the mParivahan RTO app, spread via WhatsApp and SMS smishing with shortened URLs. Droppers use ZIP manipulation and native packers; a fake UPI payment flow harvests the UPI PIN, and banking SMS is exfiltrated. Some variants also bundle a cryptominer. 40+ distinct samples observed.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2025-09 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Unattributed, financially motivated (Cyble).

Also reported, not expressed as STIX patterns: Telegram bot GhostBatRat_bot.

Infrastructure context, not indicators (legitimate or shared services the campaign abused; do not block): raw.githubusercontent.com; github.com (releases); Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM); Telegram Bot API.

Key findings: A fake ₹1 "ownership verification" UPI screen captures the UPI PIN and sends it to a Firebase endpoint. Banking SMS is exfiltrated and incoming SMS can be forwarded to an attacker number, which hands the operators OTPs and UPI device binding. Payloads are pulled from GitHub; droppers use ZIP-header manipulation and native packers, and terminate on x86 emulators. Device registration runs through a Telegram bot; some variants also run a cryptominer.

objects.description:
Ads and messages offering work from home ('ghar baithe job') lead to an agent on WhatsApp or Telegram who pays small commissions for liking videos or rating places, then moves the victim to 'prepaid' task sets that need ever larger deposits until the money is frozen. In 2023 the government blocked more than 100 such websites, and Hyderabad police traced one network to Rs 712 crore taken from about 15,000 people.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2023 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Overseas-run networks using Indian mule accounts (MHA; Hyderabad Police).

Infrastructure context, not indicators (legitimate or shared services the campaign abused; do not block): Telegram; WhatsApp; Google and Meta ads.

Key findings: In December 2023, MeitY blocked more than 100 websites running task-based job and investment fraud, on the recommendation of I4C's National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit. The ads ran on Google and Meta in several languages. MHA said the sites were run by overseas actors, with proceeds moved out through card networks, cryptocurrency, overseas ATM withdrawals and international fintech companies. Hyderabad Police (July 2023): a 'rate and review' scheme on Telegram took about Rs 712 crore from some 15,000 people. Money ran through 33 shell companies and 61 bank accounts to Dubai and was converted to cryptocurrency; police said part of it reached a wallet labelled as linked to a terror group. Nine people were arrested. The hook is the early payout: real small commissions build trust before the 'prepaid' tasks start.

objects.description:
Callers posing as police, CBI, narcotics, customs, RBI or ED officers tell the victim a parcel in their name held drugs or fake passports, or that their account is tied to money laundering, then keep them on a video call under 'digital arrest' until they transfer their savings for 'verification'. I4C data shows cases rising from 39,925 in 2022 to 1,23,672 in 2024, with losses of Rs 1,918 crore that year, before falling in 2025. Much of it is run from scam compounds in Southeast Asia.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2022 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Organised scam networks, largely operating from Southeast Asia (I4C/MHA).

Key findings: I4C figures compiled by ThePrint: 39,925 cases and Rs 91 crore lost in 2022; 60,676 and Rs 339 crore in 2023; 1,23,672 and Rs 1,918 crore in 2024; then 17,264 cases and Rs 644 crore in 2025. The scripts rely on fear and isolation: a fake parcel or case, a 'senior officer' on video, uniforms and studio sets made to look like police stations, and instructions not to tell anyone or end the call. In May 2024, I4C and Microsoft blocked more than 1,000 Skype IDs used for these calls. By November 2024, more than 6.69 lakh SIM cards, 1.32 lakh IMEIs and 17,000 WhatsApp accounts linked to Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Myanmar had been blocked. On 1 December 2025, the Supreme Court directed the CBI to investigate digital-arrest cases nationwide, including the role of bank staff in opening mule accounts, and asked the RBI how it detects them. Money moves through mule accounts; the share of defrauded money blocked in time rose from 6% in 2021 to 19% by 2026.

objects.description:
After the Pahalgam attack on 22 April 2025 and India's Operation Sindoor strikes on 7 May, dozens of hacktivist groups from Pakistan, Bangladesh, Southeast Asia, the Middle East and North Africa rallied under #OpIndia. Maharashtra Cyber counted about 15 lakh attacks on Indian sites, of which 150 succeeded. Analysts who checked the headline claims found brief DDoS outages, a handful of defacements and leak claims that were mostly overstated, recycled or fabricated. The serious threat in the same weeks was APT36's targeted phishing.

Period: 2025-04-22 to 2025-06.

Claims, with the verification status the cited source reached: 2025-05: SYLHET GANG-SG and DieNet claim 247 GB stolen from the National Informatics Centre. [overstated: The 1.5 GB sample was public marketing material and media files.] 2025-05-08: Team Azrael claims more than a million Election Commission records. [recycled: The data had leaked in 2023; it does contain genuine personal data.] 2025-05: SYLHET GANG-SG claims a million case records from the Andhra Pradesh High Court. [partly-true: Mostly public case metadata, but some password hashes were exposed.] 2025-05-07: Team Azrael claims a leak of Indian Army personnel data. [false: Names, emails and phone numbers did not match; likely fabricated or misattributed.] 2025-05-07: DDoS on the PMO, the President's site and several ministries. [overstated: Downtime was likely under five minutes.] 2025-05-08: Vulture and Electronic Army Special Forces claim to have taken down CERT-In and the NTA. [false: Both sites stayed up with no observable outage.] 2025-05: KAL EGY 319 claims about 40 education and healthcare defacements. [overstated: The named sites were working normally when checked.] 2025-05: Claims of attacks on the power grid, statewide blackouts, satellite jamming, Northern Command and a BrahMos storage site. [false: Listed by Maharashtra Cyber among false claims circulated during the conflict.] 2025-05: Defacement of the Kulgaon Badlapur Municipal Council and the Defence Nursing College, Jalandhar websites. [confirmed: Reported by Maharashtra Cyber.]

Key findings: Maharashtra Cyber's 'Road of Sindoor' report counted about 15 lakh attacks on Indian critical-infrastructure websites from seven groups, including APT36, Pakistan Cyber Force, Team Insane PK, Mysterious Bangladesh and HOAX1337. Only 150 succeeded. It traced origins to Pakistan, Bangladesh, the Middle East, Indonesia and Morocco. Seqrite logged more than 650 confirmed DDoS and defacement events from over 35 groups, seven of them new, between 7 and 10 May, including attempted breaches at AIIMS and DRDO hospitals and probes against Jio and BSNL. Cyble tracked more than 40 groups. Just over half of known attacks were DDoS and about 36% defacements. NSFOCUS saw attacks on India rise about 500% after 22 April. Radware counted 256 claimed DDoS attacks on 100 Indian organisations from 26 groups in 2025 up to 8 May, peaking at seven claims an hour on the evening of 7 May. Government bodies drew over 75% of claims on 6-7 May. CloudSEK found most outages lasted under five minutes and most leak claims were exaggerated, recycled or fake. Their impact was psychological: X accounts amplified unverified claims for propaganda. CERT-In issued advisories to the financial sector, and the BSE and NSE temporarily restricted access from overseas IP addresses. India-aligned groups such as Indian Cyber Force hit back at Pakistani targets in the same period.

objects.description:
A fake digital wedding invitation, sent on WhatsApp from a known contact, that is really an Android app. Once installed it walks the victim through granting SMS, notification and 'full control' access, then runs the SpyMax remote-access trojan to read bank OTPs, WhatsApp messages and keystrokes. Maharashtra Cyber Police warned about the lure in December 2024, and K7 Labs and Broadcom analysed samples in June 2025.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2024-12 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Unattributed, financially motivated.

Also reported, not expressed as STIX patterns: Android package com.cristal.bristral.tristal.mistral; Android package com.android.pictach.

Infrastructure context, not indicators (legitimate or shared services the campaign abused; do not block): WhatsApp (delivery); Telegram Bot API.

Key findings: The file arrives as 'Wedding Invitation.apk'. It asks for SMS and contacts access, to be the default home app, and for 'Install unknown apps', then shows a fake Google Play services page asking for 'full control of your device' (K7 Labs). It installs a second package and intercepts notifications, which hands the operators bank OTPs, WhatsApp messages and 2FA codes. It also logs keystrokes, collects SMS and clipboard data, and checks for installed mobile security products. Stolen data is gzip-compressed before it is sent. K7 reported a C2 at 104.234.167[.]145 on port 7860; Broadcom saw exfiltration mainly through Telegram bots, with C2 servers as fallback. The second package's manifest references Airtel, Jio and BSNL, consistent with Indian targeting. Maharashtra Cyber Police warned citizens about fake wedding-invitation APKs in December 2024.

e-Challan / RTO-themed two-stage dropper. A fake 'update' prompt installs a second APK that hides its icon (INFO category), collects Aadhaar/PAN and full card/UPI details via fake payment screens, and intercepts incoming SMS for OTP harvesting. C2 over HTTP POST to jsonserv domains.

Attribution as reported: Unattributed, financially motivated (CYFIRMA).

Fake e-Challan and ₹1 "verification" screens collect Aadhaar, PAN, full card data, ATM PIN, net-banking credentials and UPI PIN; the UPI payment is rigged to fail. Social media ads and messages pull victims into WhatsApp or Telegram 'investment' groups run by people posing as market experts, brokers or SEBI-registered advisers. Members are coached into a fake trading app or website that shows growing profits, keep depositing, and find they cannot withdraw. I4C counted more than 30,000 victims and over Rs 1,500 crore lost in six months to October 2025.

Status in the tracker: active (describes the reporting, not whether infrastructure is live).

First reported: 2024 (precision as given by the source).

Attribution as reported: Organised fraud networks, often tied to foreign syndicates (I4C).

Infrastructure context, not indicators (legitimate or shared services the campaign abused; do not block): WhatsApp groups; Telegram channels; Facebook ads.

Key findings: I4C (October 2025): more than 30,000 victims and over Rs 1,500 crore lost in six months. Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Hyderabad account for nearly 65% of cases, and 76% of victims are aged 30 to 60. CloudSEK (July 2024) counted over 29,000 malicious investment ads on Facebook and over 81,000 fake investment WhatsApp groups since January 2024, across India, Malaysia, the US, Thailand and Vietnam. Groups are run by teams with set roles, including impersonators, hype-makers and affiliates, and show scripted 'live training' and fake proof of gains. The trading apps imitate real platforms, display fabricated profits to draw bigger deposits, and then block withdrawals. Victim data such as phone numbers of known traders is bought from brokers who source it from underground forums.

objects.description:
A Pakistan-nexus espionage actor that mimics the SideWinder group's TTPs (hence the name) and is widely assessed to overlap with Transparent Tribe/APT36 infrastructure. It targets Indian government, defence and increasingly academic and research institutions. Typical delivery is a ZIP archive embedding an LNK or decoy document that leads to RATs such as ActionRAT, AllaKore and AuTo Stealer, hosted on compromised domains.

Reported attribution: Pakistan-nexus. Linked to the Pakistan-nexus cluster through infrastructure and tooling overlap with Transparent Tribe; the group deliberately mimics SideWinder's TTPs to mislead attribution.

Key findings: The signature chain is a ZIP archive containing an LNK or decoy document that starts a multi-stage infection. Next stages are usually pulled from compromised legitimate websites rather than attacker-registered infrastructure. Payloads rotate between ActionRAT, AllaKore RAT, ReverseRAT and AuTo Stealer, which collects Office files, PDFs, databases and images. Has exploited the WinRAR flaw CVE-2023-38831, where opening a decoy file inside a crafted archive runs the payload, and fielded a Linux variant of Ares RAT (Seqrite, Nov 2023). The first public report (Seqrite, September 2020) already showed the hallmarks still seen today: LNK files with double extensions such as 'Defence-Production-Policy-2020.docx.lnk', HTA stages run through mshta, and DLL side-loading through a legitimate Windows binary.

Timeline: 2020-09: Quick Heal's Seqrite discloses 'Operation SideCopy', active since at least 2019 against Indian defence units: LNK files run HTA stages through mshta, credwiz.exe side-loads a malicious DUser.dll, and an AllaKore-based RAT or Crimson RAT follows. It assesses a Pakistani origin, likely linked to Transparent Tribe. 2023-11: Seqrite reports SideCopy exploiting the WinRAR flaw CVE-2023-38831 and fielding a Linux variant of Ares RAT. 2025-05: During Operation Sindoor, Seqrite attributes part of the Pahalgam-themed phishing against Indian defence and government to APT36 and SideCopy and ships SideCopy-specific detections.

objects.description:
A long-running espionage actor that primarily targets Indian government, defence and education sectors. Typical tradecraft is spear-phishing with weaponised documents and LNK files, and fake or trojanised apps, delivering RATs such as Crimson RAT, CapraRAT (Android) and Poseidon. 2026 reporting describes new RAT activity, LNK-based delivery chains, and expansion toward India's startup ecosystem.

Reported attribution: Pakistan-nexus. Pakistan-nexus is the consensus of vendor reporting and MITRE ATT&CK. The tracker's confidence rates the evidence for the activity described here, not the attribution.

Key findings: January 2026 campaigns sent a ZIP with an LNK disguised as a PDF; the LNK runs a remote HTA through mshta, which loads the RAT in memory and opens a decoy PDF. February 2026: Acronis TRU attributed, with high confidence, a Crimson RAT campaign against Indian startups, particularly OSINT and cybersecurity firms, delivered as an ISO containing an LNK disguised as an Excel file. Crimson RAT, a .NET RAT delivered through macro documents, remains the workhorse: file theft, screenshots, keylogging and command execution. CapraRAT extends operations to Android through trojanised or fake apps. Delivery has moved from macro documents to OLE and LNK-based chains, with repeated experiments targeting Linux desktops used in Indian government. During the April-May 2025 India-Pakistan crisis, CloudSEK and Seqrite separated this group's phishing from the hacktivist noise: Pahalgam-themed .ppam, .xlam, .lnk and .msi lures, spoofed Indian defence domains, and Crimson RAT or Ares payloads aimed at government and defence users. CloudSEK rated it the more serious threat of the period.

Timeline: 2016-03: Proofpoint publishes 'Operation Transparent Tribe': RTF documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158, watering holes and fake India-focused news sites deliver MSIL/Crimson to Indian diplomats in Saudi Arabia and Kazakhstan and to military personnel. 2023-04: SentinelLabs documents a push into Indian education: 'assignment'-themed Office documents from July to September 2022 drop Crimson RAT, with OLE embedding added alongside macros. 2025-04: Within days of the 22 April Pahalgam attack, Pahalgam-themed PowerPoint add-ins and PDFs target Indian government and defence staff, with lookalike Indian Air Force and J&K Police domains and Crimson RAT. 2026-01: LNK files disguised as PDFs inside ZIP archives run a remote HTA through mshta and load the RAT in memory. 2026-02: Acronis attributes a Crimson RAT campaign against Indian startups, especially OSINT and cybersecurity firms, to the group with high confidence.

objects.description:
A long-running Iranian espionage actor whose main focus is the Middle East, with India named repeatedly among its secondary targets: in its first documented campaigns in 2017, and in a 2023–2024 campaign that sent small businesses in India phishing links to legitimate remote-access software. It is still active in 2026, and DSCI's March 2026 advisory lists it among the Iranian state actors Indian organisations should watch after the Iran war began. No India-specific campaign has been publicly reported; India appears in multi-country target lists.

Reported attribution: Iran-nexus. US Cyber Command (January 2022) and a joint US/UK advisory (February 2022) describe MuddyWater as a subordinate element of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS); MITRE ATT&CK and vendor reporting agree. The tracker's confidence rates the evidence for activity against India, not the attribution.

Key findings: Palo Alto Unit 42's first public report on the group (November 2017) lists India among the countries targeted or suspected to be targeted from February to October 2017, alongside Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Israel, the UAE, Georgia, Pakistan, Turkey and the US. Delivery was macro-enabled Word documents dropping the POWERSTATS PowerShell backdoor. HarfangLab (April 2024) documented an October 2023 to April 2024 campaign against small businesses in Israel, India, Algeria, Turkey, Italy and Egypt, across sectors including airlines, IT, telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, logistics and travel. Using signed, legitimate remote-management software gives the group a foothold that most antivirus will not flag. In 2025, Group-IB reported a campaign against more than 100 government entities in the Middle East and North Africa using a compromised mailbox, macro documents and the Phoenix backdoor. India was not named. In 2026, Symantec and Carbon Black reported intrusions at nine organisations in nine countries using DLL side-loading through legitimately signed binaries, a Node.js implant chain, browser credential theft (ChromElevator), SAM hive theft and SOCKS5 tunnelling. The named victim was in South Korea; India was not named. DSCI's March 2026 advisory on the Middle East conflict lists MuddyWater, with APT33, APT34, Handala and CyberAv3ngers, among the Iranian actors posing risk to Indian organisations, especially IT/ITeS firms with Gulf, Israeli or Western clients. It does not report a specific MuddyWater intrusion in India.

objects.description:
China-nexus intrusions against India's power grid. Recorded Future disclosed RedEcho in February 2021 after it targeted ten Indian power-sector organisations, including four of the five Regional Load Despatch Centres, and two seaports with the ShadowPad backdoor. In April 2022 it reported a separate cluster, TAG-38, inside at least seven State Load Despatch Centres near Ladakh, using hacked DVR and IP cameras as command-and-control relays. Both periods followed India-China border tension.

Reported attribution: China-nexus. Recorded Future assesses RedEcho as China-linked and notes overlaps with APT41 and Tonto Team infrastructure, but says the evidence is not enough to attribute it firmly to either; MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as G1042. TAG-38 is a different cluster that Recorded Future could not link to RedEcho; it is kept in this entry because it targeted the same assets. China denied both.

Key findings: RedEcho (Recorded Future, February 2021): 21 IP addresses at ten Indian power generation and transmission organisations, including four of the five Regional Load Despatch Centres, a high-voltage substation and a coal-fired thermal plant, plus two seaports, communicated with ShadowPad infrastructure Recorded Future tracks as AXIOMATICASYMPTOTE. The activity rose after the India-China border clashes of May 2020. Three of the targeted Indian IP addresses had been hit in a November 2020 APT41 campaign against Indian oil and gas organisations. Maharashtra's cyber cell linked the October 2020 Mumbai blackout to malware at a State Load Despatch Centre. Recorded Future called the link to that outage unsubstantiated, so the tracker does not treat the outage as a confirmed cyber attack. TAG-38 (Recorded Future, April 2022): at least seven State Load Despatch Centres near the Ladakh border, a national emergency response system and the Indian subsidiary of a multinational logistics company. ShadowPad was controlled through likely compromised internet-facing DVR and IP camera devices, with the open-source FastReverseProxy. India's Power Minister said two attempts on load despatch centres near Ladakh were 'not successful'.

Timeline: 2020-05: Targeting of the Indian power sector rises after the India-China border clashes. 2020-10: Mumbai blackout. Maharashtra's cyber cell points to malware at a load despatch centre; the link to RedEcho is not substantiated. 2021-02: Recorded Future discloses RedEcho: ten power-sector organisations and two seaports. 2022-04: Recorded Future reports TAG-38 inside at least seven State Load Despatch Centres near Ladakh; India says the attempts failed.

objects.description:
North Korea's state hacking apparatus, which steals money for the regime and spies for strategic intelligence. India has seen both sides. The DTrack spyware and its ATM-focused sibling ATMDtrack were found in Indian banks and research centres in 2018 and 2019, and DTrack was confirmed on the administrative network of the Kudankulam nuclear power plant in 2019. In July 2024, US$235 million was drained from the Indian exchange WazirX, a theft the US, Japan and South Korea attribute to North Korea.

Reported attribution: DPRK-nexus (North Korea). The US, Japan and South Korea attribute the July 2024 WazirX theft to North Korea in a joint statement of 14 January 2025, which names the Lazarus Group among the DPRK actors the three countries have designated. The DTrack findings (Kaspersky) and the Cosmos Bank attribution (Securonix) come from vendors. Public reporting uses 'Lazarus' loosely for several DPRK clusters; MITRE ATT&CK tracks APT38 and Andariel separately.

Key findings: Kaspersky (September 2019): ATMDtrack, found in 2018, was built to get into Indian ATMs and steal card data. Code overlaps led to more than 180 samples of DTrack, a remote-access spy tool used against Indian financial institutions and research centres: keylogging, browser history, process and network listing, and file upload and download. It shares code with the 2013 DarkSeoul campaign attributed to Lazarus. Kaspersky (October 2019) found DTrack samples across 18 Indian states, led by Maharashtra (24%), Karnataka (18.5%) and Telangana (12%). Kudankulam: CERT-In notified NPCIL on 4 September 2019. After first denying any infection, NPCIL confirmed on 30 October that malware was found on the plant's administrative network, which it said is isolated from the plant systems. The malware was DTrack. Cosmos Bank, Pune (10-13 August 2018): about Rs 94 crore stolen, roughly US$11.5 million through some 14,800 ATM withdrawals in 28 countries with cloned cards approved by a malicious proxy switch, plus about US$2 million in three SWIFT transfers to a Hong Kong account. Securonix attributed it to Lazarus; there is no government attribution. WazirX (18 July 2024): about US$235 million was drained from a multisig wallet held with Liminal Custody after the attackers altered the wallet's controlling contract while signers approved transactions. WazirX and Liminal dispute where the compromise happened. Elliptic tied it to North Korea the same day. WazirX resumed trading on 24 October 2025 under a Singapore court-sanctioned scheme that returned about 85% of users' balances.

Timeline: 2018-08: Cosmos Bank, Pune, loses about Rs 94 crore through ATM cash-outs in 28 countries and SWIFT transfers; Securonix attributes it to Lazarus. 2019-09: Kaspersky publishes DTrack and ATMDtrack, found in Indian banks and research centres. 2019-09-04: CERT-In notifies NPCIL of malware linked to Kudankulam. 2019-10-30: NPCIL confirms DTrack on Kudankulam's administrative network. 2024-07-18: About US$235 million drained from WazirX. 2025-01-14: The US, Japan and South Korea attribute the WazirX theft to North Korea. 2025-10-24: WazirX resumes operations after its restructuring.

objects.description:
A China-based espionage group that turned on India in 2026. From March it sent Indian banks help-file attachments posing as HDFC Bank support tickets that installed the LOTUSLITE backdoor. In June it got into Indian government networks, including machines used by senior administrative staff, with lures about hydropower cooperation and an India-Taiwan memorandum of understanding, using Zoho WorkDrive as its command channel. Acronis, which reported both campaigns, worked with CERT-In on notification and clean-up.

Reported attribution: China-nexus. Acronis attributes the June 2026 government and energy campaign to Mustang Panda with high confidence, citing code shared with the group's TONESHELL backdoor, command servers in a network block IBM X-Force tied to the group, and a reused side-loading chain. The April 2026 banking activity rests on shared code and infrastructure. MITRE ATT&CK describes Mustang Panda as a China-based espionage actor active since at least 2012.

Key findings: Banking (Acronis, April 2026): a compiled help file, 'Request for Support.chm', bundles a legitimate executable, a rogue DLL and a page with a pop-up referencing HDFC Bank Limited. Clicking 'Yes' fetches JavaScript from cosmosmusic[.]com, which side-loads the updated LOTUSLITE (dnx.onecore.dll) through a Microsoft-signed binary. HDFC Bank is the impersonated brand, not a reported victim. LOTUSLITE talks HTTPS to a dynamic-DNS server, editor.gleeze[.]com, and gives the operators a remote shell, file operations and session management. The new build changes the traffic 'magic value' from 0x8899AABB to 0xB2EBCFDF but keeps old internal names such as KugouMain and DataImporterMain. The same build reached South Korean and US policy circles through a spoofed Gmail account impersonating Victor Cha and Google Drive links. Acronis had earlier tied LOTUSLITE to Venezuela-themed spear-phishing of US government targets in January 2026, at medium confidence. Government and energy (Acronis, June 2026): two parallel campaigns used ZIP archives with hidden DLLs and lures about a hydropower cooperation proposal and an India-Taiwan institutional MoU. SHARDLOADER side-loads through signed Solid PDF Creator and Citrix Receiver binaries, then deploys MINIRECON, a reworked TONESHELL that beacons over WebSocket inside HTTPS, or ZOHOMURK. ZOHOMURK carries hardcoded Zoho OAuth credentials and uses an attacker-owned WorkDrive account as a dead drop: it reads commands from one folder and writes stolen data to another, so its traffic looks like normal cloud use. Beacons were active from 12 to 22 June 2026. Persistence was through Run keys and a scheduled task named SolidPDFPcl2Bmp, with a reported C2 domain couldinstallup[.]com. A recurring typo, 'RunOnece', appears across several implants.

Timeline: 2026-01: Acronis ties LOTUSLITE to Venezuela-themed spear-phishing of US government targets. 2026-03: The LOTUSLITE campaign against India's banking sector begins. 2026-04-22: Acronis publishes the banking and South Korea findings. 2026-06-12: MINIRECON and ZOHOMURK implants begin beaconing from Indian government networks (until 22 June). 2026-06-29: Acronis reports the government and energy campaign, coordinated with CERT-In.

objects.name: Mustang Panda

objects.description:
Analyst assessment by Sohan Kanna: judgement over the tracker's feeds, not source-reported fact.

Two things changed since October. China-nexus espionage moved from India's power grid onto its banks and government desks, with Mustang Panda reaching Indian government networks in June and banks before that. And the patching clock got shorter: an Ivanti Connect Secure chain was exploited as a zero-day in October, PHP2Shell went from leak to public exploit in days, and CERT-In now asks for exploited internet-facing flaws to be fixed within 12 hours where feasible. Underneath, fraud against citizens keeps running at industrial scale, now fed by leaked customer data as well as fake apps.

1. Fraud runs on stolen trust: apps, impersonation and leaked data (critical): Fraud against Indian citizens is the highest-volume threat on this page and the most organised. I4C counted more than 30,000 victims and over Rs 1,500 crore lost to fake stock-tip groups and trading apps in six months, and digital-arrest calls cost Rs 644 crore in 2025 even after falling sharply from 2024. Fake APKs still do the technical work: a 'wedding invitation' that installs the SpyMax RAT reads bank OTPs from notifications. In October, SBI confirmed that personal data of at least 3,897 customers (names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, addresses and internal IDs) turned up in a dark-web set of about 375,000 records. Data like that makes a fake bank or police call sound real. Banks should assume callers will know customers' details and design verification that does not rely on it.

2. Ivanti again, and a 12-hour patch window (critical): Three Ivanti Connect Secure flaws entered CISA's KEV catalog in October: an authentication bypass on 13 October, then a privilege escalation and a file-upload flaw on 30 October. Volexity documented them chained into unauthenticated root on the VPN appliance, used by a new actor (UTA0576) to pull credentials, Active Directory data and BitLocker recovery keys. Since mid-October, Cisco ASA/FTD, Fortinet, GitLab and an Atlassian flaw with an EPSS near 99% have joined the list too. CERT-In's May 2026 guidance asks for exploited internet-facing flaws to be fixed within 12 hours where feasible. For an Ivanti box that was exposed before patching, assume credential theft: patch, check integrity, and rotate what the appliance could see.

3. China-nexus espionage reached Indian banks and government (high): For years the China-nexus story in India was the power grid (RedEcho, TAG-38). In 2026 Mustang Panda widened it. From March it sent Indian banks help-file attachments dressed as HDFC Bank support tickets that installed the LOTUSLITE backdoor, and in June it was inside Indian government networks, including machines used by senior administrative staff, using hydropower and India-Taiwan lures and Zoho WorkDrive as a command channel. Acronis worked with CERT-In on clean-up. Expect the same playbook again: signed binaries side-loading DLLs, help files and ZIP archives with hidden DLLs, and command traffic that looks like a cloud service Indian offices already use.

4. PHP2Shell, Node.js and eMudhra: the web stack had a bad month (high): Two PHP flaws (PHP2Shell) leaked before the patch, gained a public exploit and entered KEV on 26 October with EPSS near 100%; PHP branches that are already out of support get no fix at all. A Brotli decoder flaw that Node.js says permits remote code execution was added on 27 October, and it is reached through what a server downloads, not just what it receives. Separately, browsers and Node.js stopped trusting eMudhra intermediate certificates after their private keys proved recoverable, and CERT-In issued an advisory. If you run PHP or Node.js, upgrade the runtime itself, and check any service that relied on the affected eMudhra intermediates.

5. Pakistan-nexus espionage continues; hacktivist claims mostly don't hold up (medium-high): Transparent Tribe and SideCopy remain the most persistent actors against Indian government, defence and education, and they move fastest around crises: within days of the Pahalgam attack in 2025 they were sending Pahalgam-themed lures. The hacktivist noise around the same events is a different matter. Of the notable claims against India tracked here, one was confirmed in full; most were overstated, recycled or false, and DDoS outages typically lasted minutes. The practical lesson: during the next India-Pakistan flashpoint, verify leak claims before reacting, and put the effort into phishing defence for government and defence users.
